Session-context dump for T357 (ollama-concurrency-limit, glm-5.2/T357.2). What the repo does not otherwise record. Speculation labelled. Per the requested categories.

## (1) What I did
- Measured the Ollama concurrency limit for glm-5.2:cloud by firing N concurrent one-shot `ollama run glm-5.2:cloud` requests (unique arithmetic, answer not in prompt, one-line answer) at N=4,5,6,8,12,16,20, each wrapped in tools/runner with a distinct MANAGENT_TASK_ID so untracked/heartbeat.jsonl records a tool-written finish ts + true wall per worker.
- Evidence committed under docs/evidence/OLLAMA-CONC/ (heartbeat-excerpt.jsonl 71 lines, per-worker-table.tsv, driver-summaries.json, 429-error-samples.txt, PROVENANCE.md).
- Report: docs/infra/agents/ollama-concurrency-2026-08-04.md. Findings: findings/T357-ollama-concurrency.json.
- Did NOT change dispatch policy (brief forbade it); no engine/source edits.

## (2) What I did NOT finish
- Did NOT cleanly settle 'live sessions vs simultaneous active exchanges' (brief question 4): the fleet was not quiet (3 live persistent ollama launch pi sessions: T353 ~9% CPU active, T357=this, T362), so the background was uncontrolled; I did not run the controlled K-idle + M-active matrix the brief described.
- Did NOT trace a live bin/ollama-subagent 429->heal end-to-end (question 3). The 429->rc=1 is observed; the heal (heal_dispatch -> managent reopen) is a code-read inference, not a live trace. Deliberately not induced against the running fleet (it would fire a real worker into the live kanban).
- Did NOT prove the queue is strictly FIFO (question 2): the staircase of grouped finishes is compatible with FIFO into a multi-slot drain, but I did not tag launch order tightly enough to prove ordering. Stated as unsettled.
- Did NOT pin an exact integer 429 threshold: clean at 16, 2 fails at 20, against a varying ~3-session background — load-dependent, stated as ~18-20.

## (3) What the next worker should know
- The quiet-fleet precondition was NOT met (the operator dispatched T352/T362 during the run; 3 live glm-5.2:cloud sessions ran throughout). A clean re-measurement on a drained fleet is the single highest-value follow-up; it tightens every number and makes the K-idle+M-active matrix possible.
- The heartbeat wall is the TRUE per-process duration; the driver's per-worker wall is inflated by sequential proc.wait() and must not be quoted (the brief's 'trust the heartbeat' bar is correct and was validated: the two 429 fails show wall 0.2-0.3s in the heartbeat but 7.9-9.2s in the driver).
- The measurement used `ollama run` one-shots, NOT bin/ollama-subagent. Deviation documented in PROVENANCE.md + the report. If the operator specifically needs the bin/ollama-subagent persistent-session path measured (the 'live sessions' dimension), that requires launching real pi agents on a quiet fleet and is a separate, heavier run.
- The 429 text is exactly: `Error: 429 Too Many Requests: too many concurrent requests`. It comes from the cloud endpoint (glm-5.2:cloud is a cloud model; /api/ps shows [] locally). Local models (qwen3.8:27b-mlx etc.) may have a different (num_parallel-based) limit and were NOT measured.

## (4) Hazards / smells, not investigated
- The runner auto-claims the row when --task-id is passed (tools/runner:659-667) and auto-dones on rc==0 (672-674). Using --task-id with a synthetic ID (T357-wN) makes the runner exit 1 before running the command (claim fails: 'task not found'). The workaround is MANAGENT_TASK_ID env (heartbeat-only, no auto-claim). Anyone reusing this probe pattern must use the env var, not --task-id.
- The runner emits a launch heartbeat (wall=-1) ONLY when a stop directive is pending; normally there is exactly one heartbeat line per run (the exit line). So per-worker START must be derived as finish_ts - wall (heartbeat ts is second-granular, so ±1s). The driver's ms-precision start is supplementary, not authoritative.
- Cloud-model cost: this run fired 4+5+6+8+12+16+20 = 71 trivial cloud requests. Negligible, but a repeated N=20 sweep on many models would add up.
- T353 (glm-5.2) was actively generating at ~9% CPU throughout; if the operator believes a worker is stalled, a `ps -o etime,command` check is more reliable than the kanban's [stalled] tag (T353's process was very much alive).
